newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece hit by wave of strikes over austerity plans.
newsitem.headline: Greece hit by wave of strikes over austerity plans.

text.p: Greece's socialist government, facing a wave of protests against its austerity policies, said on Tuesday it would not give in to a road blockade by farmers.

Doctors, civil servants, diplomats and seamen went on strike to protest against the tax-heavy budget, hours before it went to parliament, while farmers vowed to press on with their 20-day-old action and march on Athens on Thursday.

"As far as the government is concerned our position is very clear. We shall not give in. There is no room for further concessions to farmers," National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou told Reuters Television in an interview on Tuesday.
Hundreds of civil servants shouting anti-government slogans marched through central Athens to parliament, where a five-day debate on the budget begins Tuesday evening.
Seaman pressed on with a two-day strike, halting commercial transport and tourist ferries.
The budget has angered workers by clamping down on state hiring, limiting wage rises for another year, levying new taxes and eliminating hundreds of tax breaks.
Prime Minister Costas Simitis, who won September elections, has said the tough budget was essential to meet economic targets so Greece can join a single European currency by the year 2001.
He has refused to meet any demands and boldly told the farmers he would only meet them after they abandon their crippling road blockades.
Simitis, a pro-European economist, says the government has no more money to give but the farmers have dug in their heels, saying they would bring their protest to Athens.
"We will come down to Athens for a protest on Thursday. The responsibility lies with the prime minister and his government," farmers' representative Thanassis Nasikas told television.
The farmers want lower fuel prices, higher price supports, lower Value Added Tax (VAT) on their equipment and rescheduling $1.3 billion in debts.
Papandoniou said the government was deeply concerned about the effect of the barricades and hoped there would be a turning point on Thursday after the farmers come to Athens for a protest rally.
"The consequences are quite substantial," he said. "The government is really very, very worried about the situation. Our our patience is wearing thin."

He refused to be drawn on what action the government could take to get the farmers off the highways except to "stress that the government has the responsibility for the proper functioning of the country".

The Federation of Greek Industries (SEB) estimated that the economy had lost $108 million so far from the farmers' blockade alone. Almost 60 percent of those asked by SEB said their market share would be damaged permanently.

The blockade has also taken its toll on the government's popularity in public opinion polls. A poll published in Athens newspapers on Tuesday showed Simitis's popularity had dropped to 38 percent from 50 percent in December last year.

Government officials told Reuters Simitis is concerned that any concessions could lead to demands by many other groups. Since he unveiled his budget last month the streets of Athens have reverberated daily with chants of disgruntled workers.

The civil servants' strike brought much of the public sector administration to a standstill and the General Confederation of Greek Workers (GSEE) -- the biggest labour grouping -- called a three-hour solidarity stoppage for Tuesday afternoon.
Civil aviation workers, except air traffic controllers, also called an two-hour sympathy stoppage on Tuesday.
GSEE will rally outside the parliament in the evening when the budget debate begins. The vote on the budget is set for Saturday at midnight.

Workers have demanded better pensions, higher minimum wages and expressed outrage at heavier taxation. The socialists have boosted indirect taxes on items such as alcohol and swept away hundreds of tax exemptions.
